title: Modern File Systems
summary: Extent-based allocation and copy-on-write file systems — how ZFS, Btrfs, and modern ext4 push past the classic inode-and-journal model with checksums, pooling, and near-instant snapshots.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far in this group — indexed allocation, journaling — describes the classic Unix model (ext2/ext3, still mostly true of ext4). Modern file systems push two ideas further: **extents** (allocate in ranges, not block-by-block) for efficiency on today's huge files, and **copy-on-write** (ZFS, Btrfs) which never overwrites data in place at all, trading some write overhead for near-instant snapshots and built-in corruption detection.

This is the topic that separates "I know ext4 exists" from "I understand why ZFS snapshots don't take minutes to create even on a 10TB pool" — a genuinely staff-level distinction.

slides.sectionTitle: Extents: allocating in ranges instead of block-by-block
slides.markdown:
Classic indexed allocation ([File Allocation Methods](file-allocation-methods)) stores one pointer per block — a 100MB file with 4KB blocks needs 25,600 individual pointers, spread across direct and indirect blocks. An **extent** instead describes a whole contiguous run as one compact record: `(starting block, length)`. If that same 100MB file happens to be contiguous on disk, one extent record replaces all 25,600 pointers.

This matters for two reasons: far less metadata to store and read (a huge win for large files), and the file system can reason about — and try to preserve — large contiguous runs during allocation, which keeps sequential read/write performance high even as a disk fills up and fragments.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: extent-based vs block pointer allocation
slides.markdown:
![block pointers versus extents](assets/pointers-vs-extents.svg)

The metadata difference is the whole story here: 8 pointers on the left collapse into one `(start, length)` record on the right, as long as the blocks are actually contiguous. A fragmented file still needs multiple extents — one per contiguous run — but real workloads with large sequential files see dramatic metadata savings.

This is why ext4 (which added extents on top of the classic ext2/ext3 inode structure) can represent a multi-gigabyte contiguous file with a handful of extent records instead of millions of individual block pointers.

slides.sectionTitle: Copy-on-write file systems: never overwrite in place
slides.markdown:
A traditional file system **overwrites** a block in place when you modify a file — the old bytes are gone the instant the new write lands. A **copy-on-write (CoW)** file system instead writes the new version to a *different*, freshly allocated block, then atomically repoints the relevant metadata (working up through a tree of block pointers to the root) to the new block — the old block is left untouched until nothing references it anymore.

This single design choice is the source of nearly everything distinctive about ZFS and Btrfs: it makes corruption-in-place structurally impossible (an interrupted write just leaves the old data intact and unreferenced-yet, never half-overwritten), and it makes snapshots and checksums fall out almost for free, covered next.

Because a CoW file system never overwrites data, taking a **snapshot** is just: remember the current root pointer of the block tree, and don't reclaim any block still referenced by it, even after live data moves on. No data is copied at snapshot time — that's the whole trick. As the live file system continues writing new versions of blocks elsewhere (CoW's normal behavior), the snapshot's root pointer still walks to the old, unchanged blocks, showing exactly the state at snapshot time.

This is why a ZFS snapshot of a 10TB pool completes in well under a second: it's a metadata operation — save one pointer, mark a generation boundary — not a data copy. Space is only consumed later, incrementally, as blocks the snapshot references diverge from the live file system's current state.

slides.sectionTitle: ZFS and Btrfs — what they add: checksums, pooling
slides.markdown:
Beyond CoW itself, ZFS and Btrfs add two features absent from classic ext4: every block gets a **checksum** stored in its parent pointer (not alongside the block itself, which is what makes it detect corruption the disk's own error-correction misses), and **storage pooling**, which merges multiple physical disks into one flexible pool that file systems and volumes can carve space from dynamically — no separate partitioning and resizing dance required.

Pooling in particular changes the operational model: adding a disk to a ZFS pool immediately grows the space available to every file system built on it, and RAID-like redundancy (mirroring, RAID-Z) is a pool-level property rather than something bolted on with a separate volume manager (like LVM + mdadm on classic Linux setups).

slides.sectionTitle: Checksumming for silent data corruption detection
slides.markdown:
Disks occasionally return the wrong data without reporting an error — a phenomenon called **bit rot** or **silent data corruption**: a sector's magnetic or flash charge degrades slightly, and the disk's own error correction isn't strong enough to catch it, so it hands back subtly wrong bytes as if nothing happened. Classic file systems have no way to detect this at all — the corrupted bytes are simply read and used.

ZFS and Btrfs checksum every block (commonly with a fast hash like fletcher4 or SHA-256) and verify it on every read. A mismatch means corruption was detected — and if the pool has redundancy (a mirror or RAID-Z), the file system can transparently repair the bad block from a good copy, something a traditional RAID controller alone cannot do because it has no way to know *which* copy is correct without a checksum to compare against.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: traditional journaling FS vs CoW FS
slides.markdown:
| | Journaling (ext4) | Copy-on-write (ZFS, Btrfs) |
|---|---|---|
| Update model | Overwrite in place, journal protects the transition | Never overwrite; write new, then repoint |
| Crash consistency | Journal replay after a crash | Structurally consistent by construction — old data is never half-overwritten |
| Snapshots | Not built in (needs LVM snapshots underneath, which are heavier) | Native, near-instant, cheap |
| Corruption detection | None beyond what the disk itself reports | Checksums on every block, every read |
| Write overhead | Lower — one write per change (plus journal for metadata) | Higher — fragmentation-prone since data constantly relocates, though modern implementations mitigate this |
| Maturity / tooling | Extremely mature, default on most Linux distros | Mature but heavier; ZFS notably absent from mainline Linux kernel (licensing) |

**How to decide:** choose CoW (ZFS/Btrfs) when snapshot/rollback and corruption detection matter more than raw write throughput — backup servers, NAS, database hosts that want point-in-time recovery. Choose ext4 for simplicity, maturity, and slightly better raw write performance where those extra guarantees aren't worth the cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: snapshot cost, then vs later
slides.markdown:
Creating a ZFS or Btrfs snapshot itself is O(1) regardless of data size — typically single-digit milliseconds, since it's just persisting a pointer and a generation marker. The cost shows up later, amortized: every subsequent write to a block the snapshot references triggers a CoW allocation of a new block instead of an in-place overwrite, and the *old* block stays allocated (referenced by the snapshot) until that snapshot is deleted.

Concretely: keeping ten daily snapshots of a busy database means roughly ten days' worth of "before" versions of every block that changed stay on disk, which is why snapshot-heavy ZFS pools need meaningfully more free space headroom than a plain ext4 volume of the same nominal size — the cost didn't disappear, it moved from "paid upfront" to "paid gradually as data diverges."

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming CoW file systems have no downsides
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "ZFS/Btrfs are strictly better than ext4 — checksums and snapshots for free, why wouldn't everyone use them?"

**Why it's wrong:** never-overwrite-in-place means a file that's modified in small random chunks over time (a database's data file, a VM disk image) gets progressively fragmented, since each modified chunk is written to a brand-new location rather than reused in place — something a traditional in-place file system doesn't suffer from at all. CoW file systems also generally use more RAM (ZFS's ARC cache is famously memory-hungry) and carry real operational complexity (ZFS pool management is its own skill, not a drop-in ext4 replacement).

**Correct model:** CoW trades some write performance and fragmentation resistance for corruption detection and cheap snapshots — a real trade-off, not a strict upgrade. The right choice depends on whether your workload values point-in-time recovery and data integrity guarantees enough to pay for them.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: RAID-Z vs traditional RAID
slides.markdown:
Traditional RAID (hardware or `mdadm`) operates below the file system, at the block level — it has no idea which blocks are actually in use, so rebuilding a failed disk means reconstructing *every* block, used or not, and it can't tell you which copy is correct if checksums disagree (the infamous "write hole" problem in RAID 5/6, where a crash during a stripe write can leave inconsistent parity with no way to detect it).

**RAID-Z**, ZFS's answer, is integrated with the file system itself: it only rebuilds blocks that are actually allocated (often much faster on a partially-full pool), and because every block is checksummed, a resilver can verify each reconstructed block against its checksum rather than trusting parity math blindly. This tight integration — impossible for a RAID layer that sits below and doesn't know about the file system's structure — is a genuinely staff-level distinction interviewers listen for when RAID comes up in a storage-design conversation.
